status_reason: Glucose is a defined target, but viable biomass has no measurable signal or reference in the sources, and fluorescence has no direct route to glucose, so the alternative depends on facts the client has not yet provided.
answer: Fluorescence cannot report glucose directly, and its high sensitivity does not make it selective, so it is not a basis for either target. Test Raman first for glucose, with NIR as the comparison method. Treat viable biomass as a separate problem that needs an independent viability reference before any method is chosen.

inline.headline: Test Raman on in-line fermentation samples for glucose, with NIR as comparison; viable biomass waits for a viability reference
inline.probe: Raman fiber probe; excitation 785 nm in the cited pharmaceutical example, to be chosen in the lab; spectral axis in Raman shift (cm-1)
inline.install: In the fermentation vessel through a port or sampling loop, with the spectrometer remote from the vessel; port position not stated by the client
inline.fiber: Al/Cu-coated silica fiber in the Vis-NIR silica range (350-2400 nm)
inline.test_against: NIR transmission or transflection probe for glucose in the millimolar range
inline.not_final_because: No Raman or NIR glucose data exist yet; fluorescence background can mask Raman in many organic compounds; the fermentation matrix is unknown; no viable-biomass reference is defined.

problems.text: Sensitivity is not selectivity: fluorimetry is rated high in sensitivity but low in selectivity, and it relies on substances that fluoresce, which most chemicals do not.
Glucose has no direct fluorescence route: the sources assign glucose to NIR and Raman, while fluorescence targets intrinsic fluorophores such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin.

Viable biomass needs a defined signal and a reference: the sources link biomass to turbidity (cell density) and report that NIR combined with fluorescence improved biomass in yeast, but describe no viable-cell measurement, so a viability reference is required.

methods.why: Gives direct detection of glucose in aqueous media, the closest route to the glucose target; needs special probes and filtering against fluorescence.
Tracks glucose in the millimolar range, the standard online fiber-probe method, but may lack sensitivity below 0.1 %.
No direct glucose route and no fluorescent biomass marker has been identified.
Turbidity correlates with cell density, a low-cost biomass proxy that does not measure viability.

questions.q: Which independent viable-cell reference method will you use to define viable biomass?
questions.why: The sources describe no viable-cell measurement, so no model can be validated without one.

questions.q: What glucose concentration range and fermentation medium (turbidity, cell density) do you run?
questions.why: NIR suits millimolar glucose but not trace levels, and fluorescence background can mask Raman in some media.

questions.q: Could you run a fluorescence scan of broth samples to check for any usable fluorescent component?
questions.why: The combined-probe work is limited to samples with at least one fluorescent component.

questions.q: What accuracy and failure limits must the glucose and biomass reports meet?
questions.why: Chemometric models must be built and validated against these limits before use.

questions.q: Is there a vessel port or sampling loop where a Raman or NIR probe can be mounted?
questions.why: Fiber optics allow the spectrometer to sit away from the process, but the probe still needs an installation point.

experiment.objective: Decide whether Raman, with NIR as comparison, can report glucose during fermentation, and whether any method can report viable biomass once a reference exists.
steps: Take fermentation samples across the run and scan them on the existing fluorescence spectrometer to check for a usable signal.
Record Raman and NIR spectra of the same samples with synchronised probes.
Measure glucose and viable cell count by independent laboratory analyses; these are references, not instrument calibration.
Build a chemometric model per method and validate it on held-out batches.
Compare the fused NIR plus Raman model with the best single method on the same validation data.
references: S01 p.5 chemometric calibration and validation
S01 p.14-15 NIR plus Raman feed-frame study
experiment.go_no_go: Acceptance criteria come from the client and are not set in this assessment.

pathway.key_features: Key spectral features must be identified in the lab by multivariate analysis; the sources give no glucose or biomass band positions for Raman or NIR in this process.
pathway.path_reason: No spectra, key features or model exist yet, so the lab test must come first.

multispectral.why: NIR sees hydrogen bonds and polar groups while Raman sees the molecular backbone, and both have been applied to glucose in bioprocess monitoring, so their information is complementary.
multispectral.test: Compare the fused NIR plus Raman PLS model with the best single method on the same validation data; it counts only if it beats that method.
